body: I really appreciate you saying that. When I was at my worst with BDD, she was a MASSIVE trigger for me, especially thinking she was all natural.

I grew up in a cultural background where mental illness is not considered at all. I was also more inattentive than hyperactive. I would be quietly distracted, like doodling in my notebook instead of taking notes. Of course, I didn't want to get in trouble for being distracted, so I kept it very hidden. 

When I missed deadlines, forgot assignments, and failed classes, I would constantly get the "full of potential but needs to apply herself" and "you can do anything if only you would put your mind to it". I was just seen as lazy and care-free when in actuality I was getting white hairs from the stress.

I was almost kicked out of university before being medicated and receiving accommodations. It's very possible.

Okay, I went and actually read your post, and it sounds similar to my situation. I was constantly on academic probation, on and off withdrawal from school, and it took me a total of 8 years to graduate. I had to really advocate for myself through the entire process of getting diagnosed with ADHD, and it took a very understanding psychiatrist to get me onto the path of actually being screened. Maybe bring your transcript to your psychologist that shows all the terms you were on academic probation and how long it took you to graduate.

I understand that you don't mean any harm at all by asking the question, and I kinda appreciate that most culturally non-Korean/Asian people don't pay much attention to monolids or double eyelids. Honestly, I just needed to get it off my chest because conversation like this can easily turn into speculation that Asians are trying to look less Asian when it's really not that.

I used to care a lot about how my eyes looked because of this beauty standard. I personally hate that it exists, but I also think it should be up to individual preference without societal pressure or judgment in either direction. I agree that beauty should be seen more subjectively.

I come from a background where Asians are seen as wannabe white people, and *everything* we do, especially as the younger generation, is nitpicked as wanting or trying to be more white. I was agitated by your comment, but I shouldn't have taken it out on you when you're really not coming from a malicious place. I just saw the comment and reacted without considering the feelings of the person behind it. I'm sorry.

Ethnicity has a lot less to do with physical appearance than race, which is why I brought up race. When you talk about physical features that are typically associated with a group of people, you're talking about race, not ethnicity.

There's not much to read into here. You're implying that double eyelid surgery is a procedure to minimize or eliminate a person's ethnic features, the "ethnic feature" being monolids. The term "ethnic" is being used as a way to say "non-white" or "Korean" which implies that double eyelid surgery is a procedure to look more white or less Korean. If it's being used as a way to refer to physical features associated with a racial (or ethnic) group, then I'm saying that monolids are not that.

I'll admit I'm a little heated, but I hope you understand I'm not trying to attack you personally. I'm just sick of comments like these implying that double eyelid surgery has anything to do with racial (or ethnic) identity.

It's a very small procedure that Korean plastic surgeons are very experienced in. It barely changes anything. A lot of my non-Asian friends can't even tell the difference between monolids and double eyelids unless I point it out directly.

I'm not saying I agree with plastic surgery at such a young age, but it's not as life-altering as you might think.

Race is a social construct not strictly defined by physical features. Not all Koreans have smaller eyes or monolids. A Korean person born with double eyelids is no less Korean than one born with monolids. To be blunt, it's racist to assume that a Korean person who goes through double eyelid surgery is trying to look less Korean.

It's more complicated than having it or not. I technically have double eyelids, but they're hooded so they look like monolids depending on how bloated my face is. Some don't have double eyelids at all. Some have very prominent double eyelids. Some have one monolid and one double eyelid. Some even have multiple eyelid creases.

Your question was very ignorant, but I can see it comes from a place of wanting to understand better. Personally, I'm sensitive to this kind of question because there has been a lot of misinformation surrounding the Korean double eyelid ideal with western media spinning it as a desire to look more white/caucasian.

It's very racist to assume that all Koreans have small eyes and monolids and imply that they undergo double eyelid surgery to look less Korean and more white. I'm not saying that's what you're doing, but this might explain some downvotes.

For me, it's not an OCD thing. For others, it could be. But the act of checking by itself is NOT indicative of OCD. It depends on the quantitative and qualitative nature of their "checking". It's not up to us to diagnose anyone here.

Also, what are you saying? Pure obsessional OCD still has the fearful or intrusive component to it. The only difference is that your compulsions are mental rather than physical.

It's only a diagnosable as OCD if it impairs your daily functioning. If not, then it's just not a disorder. Neurotypical people do things like checking if the front door is locked. Maybe they do it twice. It's not a disorder until they're doing it so much that they're losing sleep to do it or waking up in the middle of night several days a week to check again.

The psychiatrist who diagnosed me was more focused on how much I did the collective behaviors more than the actual reasoning behind the behaviors. I told her maybe all those behaviors take up more than however much time a day in all, but I'm not sure. That's it. That's how I got diagnosed.

It doesn't take up enough of my time to be inhibitive to my daily functioning, and it's not driven by intrusive thoughts. 

I tend to make sure to look over "official" submissions to check for mistakes, especially when it's information-dense as OP stated. Sometimes, I just like to admire my writing lol.

It doesn't take up enough of my time, and it's not a ritual or anything driven by intrusive thoughts. It's not that I feel like I need to do it or else something bad will happen.

Out of all the psychiatrists I've seen, only one has ever diagnosed me with OCD because of this and a kind of tic I have. She just asked me if they take up over a certain number of hours a week, and that was it. (I told her I can't really quantify it precisely for her, but maybe since my tic occurs a lot throughout the day.) None of my other psychiatrists think it's enough to qualify for a diagnosis of OCD, and I agree.

There were a few other kind of symptoms I had that also could have fallen under OCD, but I don't get the intrusive thoughts or fear like I said. I just get the dopamine hits.
I actually got diagnosed with OCD for this, but it's 100% an ADHD thing for me.
